entry.content:
Inkling 2 Mini is getting a lot of attention right now, so I ran it on my own open source benchmark, Delta-Bench. In Delta-Bench, an agent works on Delta Lake tables in a Databricks-style workspace: it restores damaged tables, fixes a MERGE job, changes a schema, reclusters a table, and answers questions about messy data.

I compared Inkling with two other similar sized open models, Qwen3.8-27B and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. I didn’t train any of the three. As a reference, I added echo-020, a 4B model I trained on this environment in my first post. Here is how all four models performed:

For Inkling 2 Mini, in short:

  • It comes second among the released models. It solves 59% of test-ood-hard set, the harder split, between Qwen (70%) and Lightning (32%). It is much closer to Qwen on dev set, the difference is +0.043 [-0.005, +0.094].
  • It is very uneven. It has the highest score of all four models on B, MERGE (1.00) and E, data quality (0.99), and the lowest on A, time travel (0.08). One sentence in the task is enough to take it from 52 of 52 solved to 11 of 108 (I’ll explain this in the later section).
  • This is not Inkling at its best setting. It runs at the lowest reasoning effort and under my cap of 1,024 tokens per turn, and 93 of its 328 failed rollouts on test-ood-hard end at that cap.

And across the four models:

  • Among the three untrained models, the predicting order is the reverse of the acting order. Lightning predicts best and acts worst. Qwen predicts worst and acts best.
  • echo-020 predicts best of all four. On test-ood-hard it ties with Qwen, which has almost 7 times its parameters. This is not a surprise since echo-020 was trained to predict and act.
  • The predicting score has its own problem. Qwen is more surprised by an output when the same output is already in the episode.

Why two scores? In my first post, the models trained with ECHO, which adds a loss for predicting the tool outputs, predicted better and solved more tasks than the one trained with GRPO alone. However, I couldn’t say that the first caused the second, since most of the gain looked like regularization. (echo-020 is the ECHO model with $\lambda=0.02$.) Training changes both things at once. With released models I can take the training away, and look at whether the better predictor is also the better actor.

All 6,400 rollouts are on Hugging Face, with the full conversations: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Sly6366/delta-world-predicting-acting. The dataset card lists most of the ones I quote in this post.

Setup

Models

ModelParametersPrecisionSampling
Inkling 2 Mini26.4B, 3.4B activemixed NVFP4 + MXFP8, as releasedtemperature 0.6, top-p 1.0
Qwen3.8-27B27BBF16temperature 0.7, top-p 0.8, top-k 20, presence penalty 1.5
Nemotron 3.5 Lightning30B, 3B activeBF16temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95
echo-020 (Nemotron 3 Nano, trained)4BBF16temperature 0.6, top-p 1.0

Each model runs at its vendor’s sampling setting. I didn’t find suggested sampling parameters at Inkling 2 Mini’s model card, so it uses the same setting as my 4B model. Reasoning is off for every model, with one exception: Inkling can’t turn it off completely. At its lowest setting, 70% of its turns still carry reasoning.

The tasks are the same five families as in the first post: A (time travel), B (MERGE), C (schema evolution), D (clustering) and E (data quality). The agent has the same three tools, run_sql, run_python and submit, with up to 16 turns and 1,024 new tokens per turn.

Acting Score And Prediction Score

Acting is the verifier’s result on the final table, reported as pass@1. Each model ran 200 instances on dev and 200 on test-ood-hard, with 4 samples each. That is 1,600 rollouts per model and 6,400 in total.

Predicting uses recorded episodes. I took the first dev rollout of every instance from each of the four models, 800 episodes in total, and let every model read all of them. At each tool output, I record the probability the model gave to the tokens that actually came back. All models are scored on exactly the same 6,651 outputs.

In the first post I reported nats per token. That doesn’t work across different models, because each tokenizer cuts the same text differently. Therefore I use bits per byte:

$$\text{bits per byte} = \frac{\sum -\log_2 p(\text{token})}{\text{number of bytes}}$$

Lower is better. As in the first post, I report the predictable part separately.

Acting

echo-0200.789 [0.736, 0.838]0.711 [0.653, 0.768]1.36
Qwen3.8-27B0.721 [0.665, 0.775]0.700 [0.645, 0.754]3.30
Inkling 2 Mini0.679 [0.620, 0.736]0.590 [0.526, 0.651]4.17
Nemotron 3.5 Lightning0.331 [0.278, 0.388]0.324 [0.270, 0.378]10.54

The brackets are 95% confidence intervals over instances. On test-ood-hard, echo-020 and Qwen are indistinguishable: the paired difference is +0.011 [-0.029, +0.053]. The cost is inference only, and it doesn’t include training echo-020.

The tasks each model solves in details:

echo-020 being the best here is expected, because ECHO trained it to predict exactly these outputs.

The Prediction Order is the Reverse of Acting Order

Lightning predicts best among the untrained models and solves the fewest tasks. Qwen predicts worst and solves the most.

I have only tested 3 open-weight models, therefore I couldn’t conclude that a better predictor act worse in general. In this experiment, the best untrained predictor (lightning) is the worst actor, by a wide margin.

The Full Scorecard

This is the rest of what I measured:

Two more things stand out in Inkling’s column:

  • It checks its work most often. It checks before submit in 69% of the rollouts that change something, against 64% for Qwen.
  • It talks the most. It writes 1,877 output tokens per episode, and about two thirds of them are reasoning, even though I set its reasoning effort to the lowest.

Different Model Acts Differently

One Sentence Decides Inkling’s Family A Score

Some family A tasks include the sentence “Other jobs have written to the table since then.” On dev, Inkling solves 52 of 52 without it, and 11 of 108 with it.

Every family A task in test-ood-hard has the sentence, and Inkling solves 12 of 160.

Here is Inkling on a dev task without the sentence. It reads the history, checks version 3, and restores:

And here is Inkling on a task with the sentence:

Inkling knows RESTORE well. It predicts correctly that it would discard the later rows, and uses that to argue itself out of what the task says: “exactly the state it was in immediately before that operation”. Of its 148 family A failures on test-ood-hard, 93 never change the table (81 of them hit the token cap like this one), 41 rewrite it by hand, and 14 restore it and then add a write by hand.

Lightning Predicts the Error, and Sends the Command Anyway

In this dev episode, the table is clustered on the wrong column. The number on the right is how surprised Lightning is by each output, in bits per predictable byte:

After the first syntax error, the next six cost Lightning only 0.03-0.63 bits per byte. By then it knows what will come back. On the same six errors, Inkling pays 2.4-6.1 and Qwen pays 11.5-16.3. Lightning sends the commands anyway, and it never tries ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY, which is where the fix starts.

The same thing happens in family A. Here Lightning finds the right version, and then can’t write the statement:

The statement needs TO VERSION AS OF 10. Lightning even writes AS OF in its own text, one line above. In 58 of its family A failures it tries a RESTORE and none ever runs. In 54 of these 58, the first RESTORE leaves AS OF out.

Then there is this ending, from family E:

52 is the right answer, but it has to be passed to submit. If you read the first post, this is what GRPO did after it collapsed. Lightning does it without any training from me: it has 110 family E rollouts with no submitted answer, and in 23 of them the last message has no tool call and contains the right value.

Qwen Is Surprised by What It Has Already Seen

Qwen’s predicting score is so bad that it looks like a bug in the scorer. Here is a dev episode. Qwen runs the same dashboard query three times, and the result never changes:

The first time, Qwen pays 5.95 bits per byte. The second time, with the answer already in its context, it pays 21.13. The third time, 22.10. Lightning pays 3.24, then 0.00 and 0.00.

Over all 800 episodes, 151 query results repeat an earlier one word for word. On those, Lightning drops from 1.53 to 0.03 bits per byte and echo-020 from 1.36 to 0.05. Qwen goes up, from 8.06 to 19.37.

A model that can’t assign probability to text it has just read isn’t missing knowledge about Delta Lake. My guess is that its post-training never scored the tool outputs. As I mentioned in the first post, they are usually masked in supervised fine-tuning, so nothing keeps the probabilities there meaningful. However, that can’t be the whole story, since Lightning was probably trained in a similar way and copies without trouble.

It doesn’t hurt Qwen’s acting, though. In the same episode it goes on to solve the task, with the step most models miss (OPTIMIZE FULL after OPTIMIZE):

Qwen has a different weakness: it doesn’t stop checking. In this family E task, it has the answer at turn 3:

56 is correct. Qwen has 19 family E failures without an answer, and in 15 of them the right value is in one of its own outputs.

The No-Op That Says It Did Nothing

In 21 of the 40 family D tasks on test-ood-hard, the table is already clustered, but on the wrong column. Changing the key is not enough, and a plain OPTIMIZE does nothing. The output says so:

Here are two models on this same instance. echo-020:

Inkling:

Both models read the same output. Inkling took it as evidence that nothing happened. echo-020 described a rewrite that never happened. Over the 84 rollouts each model gets on these tables, Inkling solves 24, Qwen 6, echo-020 2 and Lightning 0. All 24 of Inkling’s solves ran the plain OPTIMIZE first and then FULL.

In the second post, this was one of two kinds of task that no model learned. Inkling shows the step is not out of reach. My training almost never found it.

Does a Prediction Change the Next Action?

The comparison so far is between models. Let’s see if there is a link inside one model: when a model predicted an error well, does it act differently from when the error surprised it?

I took every first-seen error in a model’s own dev episodes, split them in half by how surprised the model was, and labelled what the model did next. Only Inkling shows a pattern that survives my checks. After a surprising error, its next call inspects something 50% of the time. It only inspects 36% of the time after an error it predicted well.

Here is one example of each:

Inkling is the only model that has this behaviour.

Conclusion

Does the best predictor act best? Among these models, no. Lightning knows what a wrong command returns, and doesn’t know the right command. Qwen assigns almost no probability to a result it has just read, and solves the most tasks of the three.

echo-020 is the only model that does well on both scores. It was also trained on both, so it can’t tell me which one helped. The way to find out is still the one from the first post: train GRPO with a KL penalty on this recipe, and compare it with the same ECHO arms.

References

  • Shrivastava et al., ECHO, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24517

entry.content:
In my previous post, I trained an LLM agent on Delta Lake tasks with GRPO and with ECHO. I compared how well each model predicts its tool outputs and how many tasks it solves. That post was already long, so I left out most of what happened on the way to those results. This post covers the problems I ran into, the training metrics that pointed to them, why I read them the way I did, and what I changed.

The setup, briefly:

  • Policy: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano 4B, non-thinking. It is a hybrid model that keeps most of its state in Mamba-2 layers and has four attention layers.
  • Training: NeMo RL 0.7 on the Megatron backend, with vLLM as the sampler. GRPO with 8 prompts × 8 rollouts per step, for 90 steps.
  • Arms: GRPO, ECHO with $\lambda=0.005$ and ECHO with $\lambda=0.02$, one seed each.
  • Hardware: each arm ran on one H200 on Modal. A run took about 4 hours and cost about $23.
  • Environment: a Databricks-style simulator built on Spark Connect and Delta Lake. The agent has three tools, run_sql, run_python and submit, and a verifier checks the final state of the tables.

The code is at munhouiani/delta_world.

Before Training

Base Model Claims Success Without Acting

Base Nemotron could not do these tasks. When I asked it to restore a damaged table, it would query the table and then claim the job was done, without ever running RESTORE. In a pilot, it ran 2 RESTOREs in 48 attempts and solved about 5% of dev tasks, none in family A (time travel) or D (clustering). Here is an example of execution:

The verifier reads the table’s final state and ignores what the agent says it did, so this episode scores 0. That is what a verifier should do, but it left RL with nothing to learn from. When all 8 rollouts in a group fail, every advantage in the group is zero, and the group contributes no gradient.

I first tried few-shot examples of the agent loop in the system prompt. That made things worse: family C (schema evolution) fell from 0.15 to 0.02.

What worked was a light supervised fine-tune on verified episodes from a teacher model, Claude Haiku 5.5, trained on the assistant’s tokens only. The amount of data has a significant impact:

Teacher episodes per familyResult
10no better than the base model
25a usable start, with every family except D above zero
1000.77 on dev, which leaves little room for RL to show anything

I used 25 per family, which I call S0. It scores 0.240 on dev and is the starting point for all three arms.

Lesson: Don’t rush into RL. Check that your base model produces a learning signal and has room to improve.

Slow Simulator

A training step waits for all 64 episodes, so at first the simulator’s speed set the cost of the whole experiment. Delta commits took most of the time: a MERGE costs about 1s and a RESTORE about 2s. Setting up and verifying a task took 65% of an episode’s time. Under load, the Spark JVM was CPU-bound, because it compiled generated code for every new query plan.

I ended up turning off Spark’s code generation and using Hadoop’s raw local filesystem. One episode went from 8.3 s to 4.5 s, and throughput at 8 concurrent episodes rose from 0.26 to 0.58 episodes per second. These changes were meant to be invisible to the agent, but the reinforcement learning cycle runs faster (and saves me a lot of money).

Lesson: The bottleneck of an RL cycle might not be GPU training. Finding and fixing it saves a lot of money.

During Training

Every run logged about a hundred metrics to Weights & Biases at each step. The default dashboard shows reward and loss, and those were rarely where a problem showed first. These are the signals that told me something:

SignalHealthyWhat I sawWhat I did
Step-1 rewardclose to S0’s pass@1 (0.240)0.27-0.33nothing
Worst sequence’s sampler/trainer probability ratioabout 1.01$10^{12}$ to $10^{24}$ on about half the early stepsstopped all arms, found the cause, relaunched
Groups where all 8 rollouts failedfallingECHO’s fell; GRPO’s fell, then rosebroke it down by family
The starting model’s habitsstableGRPO’s submit share fell from 0.45 to 0.02wrote down how to read the results
Policy entropyflat or slowly fallingECHO’s rose 2.3x and 3.2x; GRPO’s halvedwatched
ECHO’s observation lossfalling as reward risesfell while reward collapsedread it next to truncation
Training rewardtracks the evaluationmatched overall, hid a lost familyevaluated by family at steps 30, 60 and 90

The First Step

Step 1 samples S0 on tasks from the same generators as the evaluation, so I expected its batch reward to land near S0’s pass@1 of 0.240. That only holds if the sampler settings match. NeMo RL’s default sampling temperature is 1.0 and my evaluation uses 0.6, so I set 0.6 before launch.

The three arms’ step-1 rewards were 0.27, 0.31 and 0.33. All three sample the same S0 on the same prompts at step 1, so their differences are sampling noise alone. A batch of 64 rollouts on only 8 prompts is close enough to 0.24, and I changed nothing. The point is to know what step 1 should show before launching, and to stop if it shows something else.

The Sampler and The Trainer Disagreed

In NeMo RL, vLLM samples the rollouts and Megatron computes the gradients, both from the same weights. The update treats the sampled tokens as if Megatron had sampled them, so if the two engines disagree, every update is off-policy. NeMo RL logs the disagreement as the generation KL error, and as max_seq_mult_prob_error, the probability ratio of the worst sequence in the batch. When the engines agree, the KL error is about 3e-4 and the worst ratio about 1.01.

At the first launch, both metrics spiked on about half of the early steps, in every arm, GRPO included. The KL error reached 0.005-0.056, and the worst sequence’s ratio reached $10^{12}$ to $10^{24}$.

A few sequences carried each spike. In the per-step sample dumps, their generation turned to garbage right after a tool result:

vLLM had sampled those tokens at a log-probability of about -0.7, and Megatron scored them at -35 to -56. 33 of GRPO’s first 512 rollouts (6.4%) were corrupted like this. Nearly all of them scored 0, so the trainer was learning from sampler garbage as if it were the policy’s own failures, and the group baselines shifted with it. I stopped all three arms at steps 10-13.

My first diagnosis was wrong. vLLM’s start-up log warned that prefix caching on this hybrid model caches the Mamba state in an experimental mode. Multi-turn rollouts reuse prefixes all the time, so prefix caching looked like the cause, and I turned it off. Corruption went from 6% of rollouts to 52%, on every step. Without the cache, every long prefill ran in 2,048-token chunks.

So I stopped guessing and changed one setting at a time, in 4-step runs, counting corrupted rollouts directly from the sample dumps. A rollout counted as corrupted if any of its tokens differed between the two engines by more than 10 nats.

Prefix cachingPrefill chunksCUDA graphsCorrupted rollouts
on2,048on (the first launch)33/512 (6%)
off2,048on265/512 (52%)
off8,192on13/256 (5%, all in step 1)
on8,192on0/256 (only 4 steps, not conclusive on its own)
off2,048decode only177/256 (69%)
off2,048on, eager compile backend102/256 (40%)
off2,048off (eager)0/256

The cause is vLLM’s CUDA graphs. With graphs on, every faster setting I tried corrupted rollouts. Graphs on decoding alone were the worst, so graph-captured decoding itself corrupts the Mamba state. Larger chunks and prefix caching only made bad batches rarer, which is why the first launch saw 6% and not 50%. In eager mode no rollout was corrupted, and the largest gap between the engines on any token was 0.90 nats.

Running in eager mode costs speed. During my diagnosis, steps were about 60% slower with eager mode. I had no choice but to relaunch the three arms in eager mode, and made eager the default for every vLLM in the project, to keep training correct.

Lesson: Capture, sample, and watch the worst sequence in each batch.

Groups With Nothing To Learn From

GRPO’s advantage is each rollout’s reward minus its group’s mean. A group whose 8 rollouts all fail, or all succeed, contributes no gradient. NeMo RL logs the share of each kind, and I expected the all-fail share to fall as the policy improved.

The ECHO arms followed that path, from 39-43% of groups over steps 1-10 to 10-21% from step 21 on. GRPO’s fell to 28% over steps 21-30, then rose again and ended at 35%. Groups with mixed outcomes were common from the start: 50-72% at step 1.

I learned three things from this. First, GRPO had a learning signal from step 1. That is not the sparse-reward setting that motivates ECHO, where most groups fail and the observation loss becomes the main teacher. Second, GRPO’s late rise came from a family it had lost, not from tasks it never learned. When I broke the share down by family, using NeMo RL’s per-sample logs, GRPO’s family-E groups failed outright in every batch I sampled from step 30 to step 60. The batch mean doesn’t show that. Third, the ECHO arms’ all-fail share settled at 16-20% from step 51. That floor is close to the share of training prompts that no model ever solved.

Lesson: Understand the RL algorithm.

After Training: Tasks No Model Learned

After training, I checked the instances that no model ever solved: 16 on dev and 28 on test-ood-hard, unsolved in 16 samples across S0 and the three step-90 arms. My first worry was broken tasks, but the scripted solver solves all 44. Most of them belong to two kinds of task that no model learned, before or after training:

KindSolved, devSolved, test-ood-hardWhat the models doThe step no model takes
C, a column widened from INT to BIGINT0/200/40ALTER COLUMN value TYPE BIGINT, which is rejectedenable delta.enableTypeWidening first
D, clustered on the wrong column1/48 for $\lambda=0.02$, 0/48 for the rest0/44CLUSTER BY the filtered column, then a plain OPTIMIZE, which reclusters nothingOPTIMIZE ... FULL

Their neighbours were learned. Renamed columns went from 2 of 32 for S0 to 27-30 of 32 for the trained arms, and unclustered tables went from 1 of 48 to 41-47 of 48. Each of the two failing kinds needs one Delta feature that the models almost never used. The environment gives no hint, just as Databricks doesn’t: the rejected ALTER returns the workspace’s own message, “ALTER TABLE CHANGE COLUMN is not supported for changing column value from INT to BIGINT”, which doesn’t mention type widening.

Neither loss can reach these tasks. A group whose 8 rollouts all fail gives GRPO no gradient. ECHO’s observation loss can’t help either: the missing step almost never runs, so its output is almost never there to be predicted. These tasks are 16.4% of the training prompts, and they cap every arm at about 0.86 on dev and 0.82 on test-ood-hard.

Lesson: Understand the failure and design a better guide for the model.

What I Would Put On the Dashboard From The Start

If I ran this again, these are the panels I would set up before step 1, in order:

  1. Step-1 reward against the starting model’s evaluation.
  2. The worst sequence’s sampler/trainer probability ratio, and a count of corrupted rollouts from the sample dumps.
  3. The share of groups where every rollout failed, per family.
  4. The starting model’s habits in the training batches: how episodes end, and the commands that decide each family.
  5. Policy entropy and generated length.
  6. Any auxiliary loss, next to reward and the truncation rate.
  7. Step time split into rollout and training, the number of episodes vLLM is generating through the rollout, and environment errors.
  8. A held-out evaluation every 30 steps, broken down by family.

Reward and loss alone would have missed most of the problems in this post.

entry.title: Lessons Learned From World Model Training for LLM Agent

entry.content:
Agentic reinforcement learning usually trains only on the agent’s own tokens: the commands it writes. The tool outputs it reads, such as query results, error messages and table histories, are masked out. The learning signal is one scalar reward per episode.

ECHO (Shrivastava et al., 2026) and related work (PaW) add a second signal. They put a cross-entropy loss on the observation tokens, so the model also learns to predict what the environment will say. They claim for

  • faster learning
  • better generalization
  • less need for expert demonstrations

The intuition is that an agent that knows what a command will do should choose commands better.

I chose Delta Lake tables on a Databricks-style workspace to test the idea. This is a suitable domain, since most of the small models confuse Delta with plain Parquet and get Unity Catalog names wrong.

This is a little demo of the agent in action:

A quick summary of what I found:

  • World model works. On held-out episodes, the ECHO-trained models predict the facts in tool outputs 0.64-0.77 nats per token better than the GRPO-trained one.
  • ECHO models solved more tasks. ECHO models beat GRPO by about 0.2, with confidence intervals from +0.12 to +0.29.
  • A better world model might not make a better agent.

This project is open source. Check the source at https://github.com/munhouiani/delta_world

Background

I would like to spend some time to connect pre-training to ECHO and its variants.

Pretraining

The model reads a very large amount of ordinary text. At each position it is scored on the probability it gave the token that actually came next: the cross-entropy, $−\log p$. This is where it learns language and facts, such as Japan’s capital.

Supervised Fine-Tuning

The loss is unchanged. Two things change:

  • The data: a demonstration, in the chat format the model will be used in, written by a person or a stronger model.
  • The mask: the prompt is read but not scored, so the model learns to answer, not to write questions. In an agent’s demonstration the tool outputs are usually masked too. The model learns the agent’s moves, not what the tools said.

Reinforcement Learning

This figure is actually more aligned with GRPO-styled reinforcement learning. The model won’t see any demonstration (unlike supervised-finetuning). The loop has three steps:

  1. Sample: a sampler runs the current model to answer each prompt several times.
  2. Score: a verifier gives each answer a reward. GRPO turns rewards into advantages by comparing each answer with its group: above the group’s mean is positive, below is negative.
  3. Train: the trainer, holding the same model, scores the sampled tokens. Per token, the loss is in effect fine-tuning’s $−\log p$ multiplied by the answer’s advantage $A$, with clipping that limits how far one update moves a probability. A positive $A$ makes the answer more likely, while a negative $A$ makes it less likely. The updated weights go back to the sampler.

A group whose answers all score the same has $A = 0$ and teaches nothing. In agentic RL an episode interleaves the agent’s turns with tool outputs. Only the agent’s tokens are in the loss, and one reward per episode is the only signal.

ECHO

The biggest selling point of ECHO is that ECHO requires the model to also predict the environment. GRPO reads the tool outputs but is never scored on predicting them. ECHO scores them with ordinary cross-entropy, not weighted by the advantage, multiplied by $\lambda$ and divided by the episode’s observation length.

  • What it buys: a model that predicts what a command will return has learned something about the environment, a world model, from its own rollouts.
  • What it costs: almost nothing. The logits come from the forward pass GRPO already makes, and no extra rollouts are needed.

ECHO Variants

ECHO trains on every observation token, weighted equally. Later work changes which tokens are predicted, how a miss is scored, or how much the loss weighs. Each of the following figures draw a variant from ECHO’s treatment of the tool calls. The lookup gets a fuller output (country: Japan, capital: Tokyo, time: 10:42), and a second call, submit(Tokyo), follows it.

PaW

PaW (Lu et al., 2026) changes all three.

  • Which: across an update, it drops the 25% of calls whose actions the policy was surest of, by action entropy. Their actions stay in the RL loss.
  • How: it replaces cross-entropy with a clipped mean absolute error. A token costs $1 − p$, never more than 1, and counts only where the model gave it a probability of at most 0.2. They believe a noisy observation can follow the same action in more than one way.
  • How much: the weight is one minus the group’s mean return over the maximum, so a group that always succeeds adds nothing.

DGS-WM

DGS-WM (Ran et al., 2026) keeps only what drives the agent’s next action.

  • Which: the output is split into minimal units of meaning, such as a sentence. Each unit is scored by how likely the agent’s actual next action is when that unit alone stands in for
    the output. Units more than half a standard deviation above the output’s mean are kept.
  • How much: a kept unit’s cross-entropy is weighted by one minus the model’s confidence on it, so what the model already predicts weighs less.

Qwen-AgentWorld

Instead of adding an auxiliary loss, Qwen-AgentWorld (Qwen team, 2026) trains a separate language world model.

  • Format: it trains on over 10 million trajectories. There is no policy and no reward: next-token cross-entropy on the environment’s turns is the whole objective.
  • Which: each turn gets a category from statistics such as how much the output overlaps the call. A keep ratio per category decides how much of it is scored: 100% for retrieval, 5% for an echo. Masked turns stay as context.
  • Use: the world model then simulates environments for a policy’s RL, or serves as a warm-up stage before it.

This study uses ECHO’s released loss, on every token of every tool output.

Building the Environment

In this project, building an environment costs most of the work, and most of the ways the results could have been wrong. This section describes:

  • what the agent acts on
  • how a rollout’s outcome is judged
  • how models are compared

Simulator

I want my agent learns how to operate on a Databricks workspace: runs serverless SQL and Python over Delta tables in Unity Catalog. However, using a real one as the environment is out of reach due to the following reasons:

  • Volume: one GRPO step runs 64 episodes and several hundred tool calls, and a run takes thousands of tool calls.
  • Writes and isolation: every episode needs full write access, its own tables, and isolation from the other 63.
  • Quota: the free workspace I used for ground truth was driven through a quota-aware runner at 600 calls an hour.

So the agent trains and is evaluated against a local simulator. The real workspace (my personal Databricks Free Edition account) is used only to measure how faithful that simulator is.

The core engine of the simulator is a long-lived Spark Connect server (Spark 4.2.0) with Delta Lake 4.4.1. Each episode gets its own Spark session and schema, and dropped when it ends. The server is never restarted between episodes. Every tables on a Databricks workspace is named as workspace.<schema>.<table>, therefore the engine needs to translates them to a schema unique to the episode. Physical names never appear in an observation, and two rollouts of the same task cannot see each other.

Open-source Spark behaves slightly different than Databricks serverless. Databricks uses Delta as its default table format, and open-source Spark would silently create Parquet tables with no history and no RESTORE. When an operation uses file paths outside Unity Catalog volumes, it should fail as they do on the workspace, with errors captured from it. Databricks uses three-part naming (catalog.schema.table), a direct POSIX-like filesystem paths to structure or unstructured files managed under Unity Catalog volumes (/Volumes), and their cluster and session timezone remains set to Etc/UTC, while open-source Spark has no such restrictions. Therefore, I need a translation layer that makes open-source Spark behaves like Databrick serverless.

How Agent Interact with Environment

Every agent is provided with three tools:

  • run_sql(query)
  • run_python(code). It runs in a per-episode Python kernel attached to the episode’s Spark session, like a notebook, so temp views and variables carry across cells
  • submit(answer). It ends the episode

Tasks

In this project, I designed 5 tasks families, and every task instance is generated from a seed: tables, data, history, damage and prompt.

FamilyThe taskWhat the agent must work outWhat test-ood-hard pushes
A, time travelA bad overwrite, delete or merge damaged a table, and other jobs wrote after it; restore the state just before the damage, with time travelwhich commit was the damage, from the history and its metrics6-9 commits, the good state 3-5 versions back, 2-4 distractor commits of the damage’s own kind
B, MERGEA nightly merge through a view over a staging table duplicates or drops rows; fix the view (highest seq wins; rows without an id are ignored)that staging repeats keys and has null ids, from counts and merge metrics3-5 repeated keys and 2-4 null ids in 12-20 staging rows
C, schema evolutionA batch’s schema changed (an added, widened or renamed column); load it so a stated downstream read works, changing the schema in placethe enforcement error the naive insert raises, or a rename that succeeds silently by positionlarger tables and batches
D, clusteringA dashboard query reads every file; fix the layout so it can skip most of themno clustering, or clustering on the wrong column (which a plain OPTIMIZE does not fix)60k-90k rows, and at most 15% of rows scanned instead of 25%
E, data qualityAnswer a question about a table with duplicates, NULLs and distractor columnsthe data itself400-800 rows, 20% NULLs, 30-45% dirty values, 5-12% duplicates

Here are examples from each task family.

A, Time Travel

A faulty MERGE into workspace.ops.invoices overwrote existing rows with bad values and inserted bogus rows. Other jobs have written to the table since then. Restore the table to exactly the state it was in immediately before that operation, using Delta time travel. Do not rebuild or rewrite the table by hand. Call submit when you are done.

The agent is expected to first call DESCRIBE HISTORY (agent sees all columns, only three columns are illustrated here):

The damage is version 5, so the answer is the version before it, not the one before the latest. The agent should then run

B, MERGE

A nightly job merges the staging table workspace.crm.subscribers_staging into workspace.crm.subscribers through the view workspace.crm.subscribers_updates:

MERGE INTO workspace.crm.subscribers t USING workspace.crm.subscribers_updates s ON t.id = s.id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *

Run as it is, the job fails with an error. Fix the view so that the job is correct for any staging data, under these rules: when an id appears more than once in staging, the row with the highest seq wins; rows without an id are invalid and must be ignored. Keep the job statement as it is. Then run the job once, check the result, and call submit.

The agent is expected to first check the staging table via a SELECT statement and be able to notice the staging has two kinds of bad rows.

Run as it is, the job stops on the repeated 801, which is already in the target: [DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE] Cannot perform Merge as multiple source rows matched and attempted to modify the same.... Therefore, the agent needs to run a fix that keeps the latest row per id and drops the NULL ids:

Finally, the agent will run the MERGE statement in the prompt.

The job then updates 3 rows and inserts 4.

C, Schema Evolution

A new batch has landed in workspace.events.sessions_batch, and its schema no longer matches workspace.events.sessions. Load every row of the batch into workspace.events.sessions, keeping the existing rows, so that this downstream read works:

SELECT id, label, value, device FROM workspace.events.sessions ORDER BY id

The read needs device (NULL for the existing rows). Change the table’s schema in place; do not drop or recreate it. Call submit when you are done.

The agent is expect to first use DESCRIBE statement to inspect the schema:

The agent should notice the batch has one more column than the table, so the obvious load fails:

A passing solution alters the table first, then loads the batch:

D, Clustering

This dashboard query reads far more of workspace.ads.clicks than it should, and it gets slower every week:

SELECT count(*) AS n, round(sum(amount), 2) AS total FROM workspace.ads.clicks WHERE campaign_id = 344

Fix the table’s layout so that the query can skip most of the table’s files. Keep the table and its rows as they are: do not drop, replace or rewrite it by hand, and do not delete rows. Call submit when you are done.

In this example, the table holds 39,000 rows in 5 files. DESCRIBE DETAIL shows no clustering columns, and the query reads every row. A plain OPTIMIZE changes nothing: it adds no files. A passing solution clusters on the filtered column and rewrites the layout:

The table then has 15 files, and the query reads 6.7% of its rows, under the 25% limit.

E, Data Quality

Answer a question about the table workspace.warehouse.inventory. Some rows repeat an earlier row exactly in every column except id. Drop those repeats (treating NULLs as equal to each other), then give the total of score over the remaining rows. Ignore NULLs. Investigate the table with queries, then call submit with the answer as a single value.

In this example, the table has 211 rows. Its channel column holds three values in 32 spellings, plus 20 NULLs:

The question says exactly, so the spellings must be left as they are here. A passing answer, submitted as 9194:

Verifiers

Reward for each task family is binary. When an episode end, the reward is calculated by a verifier runs in the agent’s own session. The agent never sees the verifier. The verifier inspect the the final state of the table, but never parse what the agent says it did. Family E’s submitted answer is the one exception. This is crucial as the agent might claim “restored via time travel” without actually running the RESTORE statement.

FamilyPasses only if
Athe contents equal the snapshot of the last good version, the table is the same table (same id), and every commit since setup is a RESTORE or maintenance
Btonight’s result is right; and then, with held-out staging data swapped in and the target rewound, re-running the job through the agent’s view gives the right result again
Cthe same table, no replace or overwrite commit, the expected columns and types, and the downstream read returns the expected rows
Dthe same table and contents, the filtered column among the clustering keys, only layout commits since setup, and emulated min/max data skipping reads at most 25% of rows (the fix reaches 5-11%)
Ethe answer matches: numbers within 1e-6, strings exactly, ignoring case and quotes

Training Setup

Model and Training Framework

  • Policy: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano 4B, non-thinking. It is a hybrid that carries most of its state in Mamba-2 layers, with four attention layers.
  • RL: NeMo RL 0.7 (Megatron backend), GRPO with 8 prompts × 8 rollouts per step, up to 16 turns, 1,024 new tokens per turn and an 8,192-token context.
  • Sampling: temperature 0.6 and top-p 1.0, in training and evaluation alike.
  • The sampler’s engine: vLLM, eager, with prefix caching off. With CUDA graphs on, it corrupted the hybrid model’s generation.
  • Length: 90 steps, with every arm seeing the same prompts at each step (seed 42). Checkpoints every 10 steps.
  • Hardware: each arm used one H200 and its own 32-CPU episode service.
  • Cost: a 90-step run took about 4 hours and cost about $23 on Modal.

Training Recipe

I follow ECHO’s released configuration (microsoft/echo-rl).

  • no KL penalty to the starting policy;
  • the policy loss averaged per sequence, not per token;
  • ratio clipping 0.2 on both sides.

Three Arms Ran

To test the idea, I trained 3 models:

  • GRPO
  • ECHO with $\lambda=0.005$
  • ECHO with $\lambda=0.02$

$\lambda$ is the weight for observation loss. In the paper, they use $\lambda=0.02$, and I ran an additional arm with $\lambda=0.005$, which is a quarter of it.

What Agent Reads And What Loss Trains On

Every tool result is rendered into text by one function, used identically in training and evaluation.

  • Format: tables print as col | col rows, in a deterministic order unless the query sorts them.
  • Masking: timestamps, durations, ids and storage paths become <TS>, <MS>, <ID> and <PATH>.
  • Truncation: outputs over 800 tokens keep their head and tail around ... N rows omitted ....
  • Errors: they keep their class and message and lose their stack traces.

Let’s further discuss what tokens in a tool result are predictable, and whats are not.

  • Trivial: boilerplate, and anything derivable from context. Column headers, repeated rows, and echoes of the agent’s own command or of the task text all count: Overwrite here repeats the task’s “INSERT OVERWRITE”.
  • Unpredictable: masked values such as <TS>.
  • Predictable: the rest. These are the facts the action and the table state determine, such as operation names, write modes, row and file counts, byte counts and error classes. Version numbers are trivial, since each one is the previous plus one.

During training, these three kinds of tokens are included in observation loss. However, the following sections will report predictable tokens separately. This is because a model can lower its loss on the whole output by copying headers and repeated rows from context (reward hacking). The predictable tokens are the ones a world model has to get from the action and the state.

ECHO’s loss, as released, trains on every token of every tool output’s body, except for two things: the chat template’s scaffold around each tool message, and harness messages such as the error for a malformed tool call.

Observation and Findings

ECHO Learns World Model

I took 178 dev-split episodes, which are never seen during training, feed into model checkpoints, and then measured each model’s cross-entropy on the observation tokens and predictable tokens.

ECHO $\lambda=0.005$1.250.58
ECHO $\lambda=0.02$1.130.45

The tables shows both ECHO arms are far below GRPO on predictable tokens.

To see how the improvement looks like, token by token, I took one row of DESCRIBE HISTORY output from a held-out episode, and feed it into model checkpoints. Each predictable token is shaded by how surprised each model was to see it.

TokenGRPOECHO $\lambda=0.02$

Values are surprise in nats.

  • The structural facts become near-certain. A table loaded once by an append has a WRITE in Append mode with no partitioning.
  • The exact counts stay uncertain for every model, as they should: the byte count cannot be derived from anything the agent has seen. ECHO is no better on them, and slightly worse on the row count here.

The previous probe shows how surprised model is by an output it is shown. Next, I would like to know a model can predict a failure. The next problem will let a model reads the start of a scripted demonstration and writes the next output itself, so it has to commit to what the command will do, including whether it fails.

The clearest example is from family-C. Recall that tasks from Family C are related to schema change. The task says the batch’s schema no longer matches the table, and the model has seen the schemas of both tables:

and the batch rows (808 | alpha | 8410650166, …). Three facts in those outputs decide what an insert does here:

  1. The workspace.iot.readings table stores value as int.
  2. The workspace.iot.readings_batch table holds value as bigint.
  3. The workspace.iot.readings_batch‘s values are too big for an INT, which stops at 2,147,483,647.

The next command, an INSERT statement, looks ordinary, so a model has to connect it to what it read.

and the actual result is

ECHO model gets the outcome, but names a different error class: the real error is an overflow raised by the values, not a type check. Its message uses facts 1 and 2, with no sign of fact 3. I ran multiple probes, and ECHO model predicts the failure every time, but GRPO never does.

ECHO Models Have More Tasks Solved, Mostly Through Two Habits GRPO Abandoned

Each point in the figure is a model checkpoint. Moving left means a better world model (less surprised by the observation tokens). Moving up means more tasks solved (pass@1). We can see that both ECHO models are better world models and solving more tasks.

Above figure shows pass@1 in totals, which hide the arms differ. Let’s see the result from another perspective:

We now can clearly see that GRPO and ECHO models perform almost equally good in most task families, except for family C and E. Upon checking the GRPO model at different steps, these situations are caused by GRPO forgetting its learned behaviour.

Let’s start with Family E. In short, GRPO stopped calling submit. E’s answer travels in submit. A-D are judged on the table’s state, and a turn with no tool call ends the episode, so for them submit is optional. In GRPO’s training batches:

At step 30, GRPO ended its episodes like this one, a family-A task it solved:

</think> closes a reasoning block, out of place with thinking off. On A-D this ending cost nothing; on E it cost every reward.

  • GRPO had been learning E. Its E rollouts won 13 of 24 at step 5 and 15 of 24 at steps 15 and 20. From step 30 they won none.
  • The ECHO arms learned it. They submitted more as training went on: 51 and 36 of 64 rollouts at step 30, and 0.8-0.95 later. Neither ended a turn on </think>.

For family C, GRPO stopped altering the schema first. C’s batch adds, widens or renames a column. The reliable order is to change the table’s schema, then insert. On dev at step 90:

Here is a typical GRPO failure, and ECHO $\lambda=0.02$ on the same instance:

  • GRPO reads the error, fixes its cause, and never retries. Its stated reasoning has degenerated into copied filler (“I’ll keep the existing rows.”), and it reports a load that did not happen.
  • ECHO fumbles the syntax three times, but in the right order.
  • The insert’s form is not the cause. ECHO $\lambda= 0.005$ names its target columns in every solved C episode, but ECHO $\lambda= 0.02$ inserts by position, as GRPO does: 86 of 96 episodes, 74 of them solved. GRPO’s positional inserts solve 33 of 94.
  • GRPO abandoned altering first habit. GRPO’s training batches still did altering first in 9 of 16 C rollouts at step 30, and in none of 64 at steps 60 and 90. The ECHO arms kept it and grew it, ending at 83-90% of evaluation episodes.

A Better World Model Doesn’t Stop Inventing Commands

Both ECHO arms write DESCRIBE statements that do not exist, and GRPO never does:

On D it sometimes cannot: 9 of its 96 D episodes repeat one failing call five times or more, and 44% reach the turn limit, against none for GRPO. Example taken from one dev episode:

Knowing what a parse error looks like did not stop it from producing one, again and again. ECHO $\lambda= 0.02$ ‘s D score still ties GRPO’s (0.45 against 0.46): when it gets past the opening, it clusters as well.

Less Tool Usage Is Not Guaranteed

Prior work expects the observation loss to cut turns, tool errors and tokens. Here the ECHO arms do use fewer, but family by family the difference is GRPO’s loops on C and E. On D, ECHO $\lambda= 0.02$ uses more than twice GRPO’s calls (9.5 against 4.2).

Learning Speed Is Indistinguishable

One of the method’s main claims is faster learning.

Paired with GRPO, devStep 30Step 60Step 90
ECHO $\lambda= 0.005$+0.21+0.10+0.20
… without E+0.06−0.06+0.02

… without E−0.09+0.02+0.10
  • On the families that do not depend on submit, neither arm learned faster.
  • Family A reversed for ECHO $\lambda= 0.005$ at step 60 (−0.29), and stayed behind.

Conclusion: Why The World Model May Not Be What Helped

The paper reports gains on terminal tasks with Qwen3 8B and 14B, and my ECHO arms gained too. That alone doesn’t show that a world model makes a better agent, for three reasons:

  • Most of our gain looks like regularization: the observation loss stopped GRPO’s collapse.
  • Our Delta Lake tasks lack some conditions the paper’s result depends on. Copying its recipe exactly wouldn’t change that.
  • Our test also differs from the paper’s: far fewer rollouts, a higher learning rate and a smaller model.

The released recipe has no KL penalty to the starting policy, and without one GRPO collapsed onto short outputs. GRPO model’s cross-entropy on tool output ended above its base model, entropy halved and outputs shrank to a third. It also dropped two habits its base model had: calling submit, which its base model does in 46% of dev episodes, and altering the schema before inserting, which its base model does in 66% of family C episodes.

The observation loss works against this. It trains the model to predict what the environment wrote, on every step and on the same weights the policy uses, which the policy loss doesn’t do.

Also, the observation loss doesn’t stop the model from learning. The ECHO arms submit and alter first more often than their base models do. The loss stopped the collapse, and that left RL free to strengthen the habits that win.

The way to find out is to train GRPO with a KL penalty, on this recipe, and compare it with the same ECHO arms. If it closes the gap, the effect is regularization. Any gap that remains could be the world model.
entry.summary:
Agentic reinforcement learning usually trains only on the agent’s own tokens: the commands it writes. The tool outputs it reads, such as query results, error messages and table histories, are masked out. The learning signal is one scalar reward per episode.

ECHO (Shrivastava et al., 2026) and related work (PaW) add a second signal. They put a cross-entropy loss on the observation tokens, so the model also learns to predict what the environment will say. They claim for

  • faster learning
  • better generalization
  • less need for expert demonstrations

The intuition is that an agent that knows what a command will do should choose commands better.

entry.content:
I’m writing this post mostly as a reminder to myself. Even though I learned this concept a long time ago, I still find myself coming back to these fundamentals whenever a new training technique comes along.

The Gap

Most tutorials illustrate next-token prediction like the picture on the left: text in, one token out. That’s fine as a mental model, but it doesn’t match what we see in the actual architecture and its outputs.

The actual input and output of an LLM are both sequences. Take the input “I love”. To keep things simple, one word is one token. The model returns two rows of logits:

  • Row 1 sees only “I” and predicts what comes after “I”.
  • Row 2 sees “I love” and predicts what comes after “I love”.

The causal mask makes this work. Position $t$ can attend only to positions $\le t$, so every row makes a prediction without looking at the answer.

Also note what the raw output is: logits, not tokens. Softmax turns each row into a probability distribution. Choosing a token, by argmax or by sampling, is a separate step that happens outside the model.

Let’s demonstrate with actual code.

Training Uses Every Row

During training the targets are simply the input shifted by one position. Each row is scored against the token that really comes next in the data:

PositionWhat it seesIts target
1Ilove
2I lovethe next word in the data, e.g. “cats”

So one forward pass over $T$ tokens gives $T$ training signals, all computed in parallel. Every position is a training example. This is why transformers train so efficiently.

We can see this actual code at HuggingFace’s transformers library:

On an older version of transfomers library, before the loss was moved into a shared function, the lines are even more readable. The following snippet is taken from modeling_llama.py of version 4.44.2:

Everything Else is a Variation

Every other stage, be it SFT, knowlege distillation or RL, does the same thing: feed a sequence in, get one distribution per position back, apply cross entropy. The only change is which positions count, what the target is, and how much each position weighs.

StagePositions that countTarget at each positionWeight
Pretraining, mid-trainingAllNext token in the data1
SFTAssistant tokensNext token in the data1
Knowledge distillationAssistant tokensThe teacher’s full distribution1
RL (GRPO)Tokens the model generatedThe token the model sampledThe rollout’s advantage $A$

Thanks.
